pieces.title: How Safe Are the Subways?
pieces.author: Paul Reeping
pieces.dek: Putting the numbers in context

posts.text: Paul Reeping argues that subway crime stays rare on any single ride, but with ridership 25% below 2019, the same crime counts now mean more risk per trip. Assaults are the category that has risen.
Read @paulreeping on how safe the subways are. He built a tool that turns reported crime rates into odds based on how often you ride, and compares New York with other transit systems.
How does New York's subway compare with other big systems? Paul Reeping finds it has the lowest reported aggravated assault rate per million rides among seven large U.S. systems he examined.

pieces.title: The Urban Optimist’s Holiday Gift Guide
pieces.author: Vital City
pieces.dek: For the New Yorker (or other metropolitan resident) who loves cities, believes in their future and wants gifts with civic soul. Our second annual edition.

posts.text: Vital City's second annual gift guide says some readers would rather give a book about parking than a scented candle. This year's list runs from Mason Williams on 50 years of New York to a tiny radiator.
Vital City's holiday gift guide: 13 books, a library card that costs nothing, retired subway signs from New York City Transit and a Knicks championship bomber. Nothing in it is sponsored.
What do you give the New Yorker who loves cities? Vital City's guide suggests a Citi Bike membership, a live subway map or "I Finished the Power Broker" mug. Nothing is sponsored.

pieces.title: Editor’s Note
pieces.author: Josh Greenman
pieces.dek: Cities are for people (and bots)

posts.text: Josh Greenman says the issue asks what AI can do for cities, and what risks it poses. The essays disagree on who should regulate it: Washington, or cities because Washington won't.
Read Josh Greenman on a New York City issue about AI that weighs government efficiency against the pitfalls, from the shuttered MyCity chatbot to 86 algorithmic tools the City now lists.
"What can these new technologies do for cities? What capabilities will they unlock? And, just as important, what risks will they pose?" Josh Greenman writes on the questions behind the issue.

pieces.title: AI and the City: A Data Story
pieces.author: Vital City
pieces.dek: How city governments, including New York, are using artificial intelligence, and where things are going next

posts.text: New York City agencies now report 86 algorithmic tools at 19 agencies, up from 31 tools at 11 in 2022, a Vital City data story finds. Local Law 35 requires the yearly accounting.
Read Vital City's data story on how city governments, New York City included, are using artificial intelligence, and where things are going next.
Which American cities tell the public exactly which algorithms their agencies use? New York City is one of a few, under Local Law 35, passed in 2022. Vital City's data story has the latest count.

pieces.title: Between Hype and Reality: What AI Can and Can’t Fix in City Hall
pieces.author: Tiffany Chu, Alicia Rouault
pieces.dek: Local governments are already putting AI to work, but that progress is only as strong as the foundation of workers and operations that it stands on.

posts.text: Tiffany Chu and Alicia Rouault argue that city governments moved paper processes onto computers but treated each upgrade as a one-time capital project. What was new is now technical debt.
Read Tiffany Chu and Alicia Rouault on what AI can and can't fix in City Hall, and why the foundation of workers and operations decides how far it gets.

"What was new is already becoming technical debt, and more people than ever are churning out of critical services because of missed administrative steps." Tiffany Chu and Alicia Rouault on AI in City Hall.

pieces.title: AI to Advance Criminal Justice Reform
pieces.author: Alex Chohlas-Wood
pieces.dek: How technology can make for fairer and more effective policing, prosecutions and jails

posts.text: Justice reforms ask swamped public servants to scrutinize more and weigh more alternatives, on top of their daily work. Alex Chohlas-Wood argues technology can carry some of that load.
Read Alex Chohlas-Wood on how AI could make policing, prosecutions and jails fairer and more effective, as New York City reforms stall and budgets tighten.
"Reforms also ask swamped public servants to do more." Alex Chohlas-Wood on why New York City's justice reforms stall, and what AI might do about it.

pieces.title: City Limits
pieces.author: Kevin Frazier
pieces.dek: Why Washington, not New York City (or state), should be the frontline regulator of AI

posts.text: Kevin Frazier argues that mayors and city councils should leave frontier AI to Washington and spend their limited resources on what only cities can do: workforce plans, AI literacy and transparent city deployments.
Read Kevin Frazier on why city officials should stay out of regulating AI labs, and what they can do instead: publish which AI tools the city uses, for what task and against which outcome measures.

"A resident cannot audit the Commerce Department, but she can walk into city hall, attend a council meeting and judge for herself whether the permit office got faster or the pothole got filled." Kevin Frazier on AI and local government.

pieces.title: The Need to Build Cities of Trust
pieces.author: Brendan O'Flaherty, Rajiv Sethi
pieces.dek: Authentication and authenticity are up for grabs in the AI age — and cities can leverage that fact to their advantage.

posts.text: As AI makes fraud cheap, Brendan O'Flaherty and Rajiv Sethi argue, face-to-face trust gains value. Cities, where people can look each other in the eye, will build whole economies around being trustworthy.
Read Brendan O'Flaherty and Rajiv Sethi on the cities of trust AI may create: finance, law, research, news and higher education clustering where handshakes and reputations still count.

"Like the Puritan dream of Boston as a shining city on a hill, the great cities of the age of AI should be shining islands of integrity in a sea of sleaze, deception and fraud." Brendan O'Flaherty and Rajiv Sethi.

pieces.title: Solving Big Problems With Big Data
pieces.author: Prem Ramaswami
pieces.dek: Our brains weren't built for city scale. AI can help.

posts.text: Prem Ramaswami argues that human minds can't trace how a two-foot road narrowing ripples through bus times, storm runoff and retail foot traffic, but minds working with AI can.
Read Prem Ramaswami on AI for city planning. He is head of Data Commons by Google and a former president of urban products at Sidewalk Labs. He lays out privacy rules cities should require.
"Data collected in the public realm must be treated as a public asset." Prem Ramaswami writes on what cities should require of sensors and AI before using either.

pieces.title: Deliverance from Bureaucratic Purgatory?
pieces.author: Julie Samuels
pieces.dek: Attack the time tax that makes government such a burden for so many New Yorkers.

posts.text: Julie Samuels argues that waiting on government is a time tax, and that someone working two shifts or managing a disability pays far more of it than someone with a flexible job and a laptop.
Read Julie Samuels on the time tax New Yorkers pay in hold music, repeated forms and applications with no way to check their status, and what city government can do about it.
"We fill out forms with information the government already has, again and again." Julie Samuels on the hours New Yorkers lose to city bureaucracy.

pieces.title: What AI Can Learn from Cities
pieces.author: Alexandros Washburn
pieces.dek: The frontier models need to embrace a new understanding of their technology.

posts.text: Alexandros Washburn argues that AI regulation should borrow from zoning, not the building code. A code checks one model. Zoning shapes what a swarm of agents does to the shared environment.
Read Alexandros Washburn on what the 1916 Zoning Resolution can teach AI regulators. In 1913 New York City's real estate titans asked for rules after one skyscraper cast its neighbors into shadow.
"A frontier is the place where you don't have neighbors yet." Alexandros Washburn on why the word is wrong for an AI industry that now has them.

pieces.title: AI to Help Students Learn and Teachers Teach
pieces.author: Justin Reich
pieces.dek: New York City's new rules provide too little room for rigorous experimentation by teachers and students.

posts.text: Justin Reich argues New York City's September AI rules for schools were set by politics. Nothing in the research changed between March and September, he writes. The vibe did.

Read Justin Reich, who has spent 25 years researching technology and learning at Harvard and MIT, on how New York City should test AI in schools: publish the outcomes it will measure and the data it will collect.
"Nothing in the science of AI and education changed between March and September." Justin Reich on why New York City's school AI policy reversed anyway.

pieces.title: AI to Improve Quality of Life
pieces.author: Josh Appel
pieces.dek: Use data to pay closer attention to delivering the services New Yorkers care most about.

posts.text: Josh Appel argues New York City already has the data to improve quality of life. What it lacks is a practical way to search it, and he says AI can supply one, starting with where to send housing inspectors.
Read Josh Appel on how artificial intelligence could point the City's inspectors, garbage trucks and night patrols to where they are needed before the complaints come in.
"City government does not need to collect an entirely new universe of information." Josh Appel on what New York City could do with the data it already has.

pieces.title: Union Members and Bots, Holding Hands
pieces.author: Stephen Goldsmith
pieces.dek: The AI bargain cities should strike with labor

posts.text: Stephen Goldsmith argues that with AI and better data, New York City can close its budget gaps by changing how government works, rather than choosing between higher taxes and cut services.
Read Stephen Goldsmith on the AI bargain the city should strike with labor, and how Mayor Mamdani's new civil service advisory committee could be the first step.
Can New York City close a projected $23 billion budget gap without raising taxes or cutting services? Stephen Goldsmith says AI and civil service reform offer a third option.

pieces.title: AI to Advance Vision Zero
pieces.author: Andrew Miller
pieces.dek: Measure streets, not just crashes

posts.text: Andrew Miller argues that New York City already has roadside sensors that count cars, bikes and mopeds and log near-misses. Vision Zero Reimagined never mentions them. He says AI could put them to work.
Read Andrew Miller on how the city could measure Vision Zero. His case: connect the cameras and sensors it already runs, add AI to read them and give a new curb office oversight.
Mayor Mamdani says he measures success by changed behavior, not tickets. How would the city know? Andrew Miller says the sensors are already on the streets and AI can make sense of what they see.

pieces.title: How New York Constrains Public Sector AI
pieces.author: Rebecca Heywood
pieces.dek: That could make cities fall behind

posts.text: Rebecca Heywood argues New York state's LOADinG Act protects the duties employees perform today, not the employees. She says that leaves agencies unable to use AI, and New York City behind other places.

Read Rebecca Heywood on how the LOADinG Act could keep New York City agencies from using AI on translation, benefits applications and permitting, while Pennsylvania, California and Ohio take a different route.
"Only New York, it seems, is explicitly protecting the duties an employee is asked to perform, not the employee themselves." Rebecca Heywood on the state's limits on public sector AI.

pieces.title: The Man at the Window
pieces.author: Carlo Ratti
pieces.dek: What algorithms can see better than people

posts.text: Carlo Ratti argues New York City should write into law the line between data about places and data about people. Collect the first freely. Collect the second only under strict conditions.
Read Carlo Ratti on what William H. Whyte's 1970s plaza cameras can teach New York City about surveillance. Ratti directs an MIT lab that has used computer vision on city streets for 20 years.

"The possibility of anonymity is one of the most important qualities that differentiate a city from a village." Carlo Ratti cites Deyan Sudjic in making the case for keeping the window and giving up the stalking.

pieces.title: How’m I Really Doing?
pieces.author: Anna Harvey
pieces.dek: Using AI to measure — and improve — city government performance

posts.text: Anna Harvey argues that AI can now do program evaluations that used to take years of data-sharing talks, so Mayor Zohran Mamdani could learn which city programs work before the next election.
Read Anna Harvey on why the Mayor's Management Report can't say whether city government is performing well. Most of its indicators track process. The rest track trends, not what a program caused.
"By the time a mayor has the results of an evaluation in hand, his next election has in all likelihood come and gone." Anna Harvey on how AI could shorten that wait.

pieces.title: The AI Time Dividend
pieces.author: Arpit Gupta
pieces.dek: Let tech give us back hours and days to do things that matter more.

posts.text: Arpit Gupta argues that AI's public image problem comes largely from the AI companies themselves, which have stressed existential risk and job losses in their own messaging.
Read Arpit Gupta on the AI time dividend: how technology could give back hours and days for things that matter more, and why public unease about AI may stand in the way.
"AI suffers from a catastrophically poor public image." Arpit Gupta writes that the companies building it have spent considerable energy stressing its existential risks and near-term job losses.

pieces.title: If Data Are Biased, AI Will Only Amplify Problems
pieces.author: Constantine Kontokosta
pieces.dek: Can artificial intelligence deliver more efficient, and fair, city public services? It depends.

posts.text: Constantine Kontokosta argues that people do not complain to city hall at the same rate, so an algorithm trained on 311 data will send help to the neighborhoods that call the most, not the ones that need it most.
Read Constantine Kontokosta on AI and city services. His lab found that pothole predictions built on 311 data in Kansas City overestimated repair needs in wealthier neighborhoods with better streets.
"Households without heat or hot water in the middle of winter are probably not going to complain about a pothole in the street." Constantine Kontokosta on why 311 data can mislead an algorithm.

pieces.title: AI to Enhance Transparency and Accountability
pieces.author: Oded Oren
pieces.dek: Open data notwithstanding, public records are not yet public knowledge.

posts.text: Oded Oren argues that large language models can turn public records into public knowledge. His group ran more than 1,700 Court of Appeals decisions through them so New Yorkers can see how each judge has ruled.
Read Oded Oren, founder of Scrutinize, on using artificial intelligence to make New York's highest court legible before the governor and state Senate fill the coming vacancies.

Why do New Yorkers know Amy Coney Barrett but not Jenny Rivera? Oded Oren says the records are public. Reading them takes expertise few people have, and he describes how artificial intelligence can supply it.

pieces.title: What Jobs Will AI Really Replace?
pieces.author: Anthony Townsend, Hugh O'Neill
pieces.dek: We built a desktop simulation to help keep the debate honest

posts.text: Anthony Townsend and Hugh O'Neill say the evidence on artificial intelligence and jobs doesn't yet tell a coherent story. Some experts see white-collar hollowing-out. Others see job growth at the biggest spenders.
Read Anthony Townsend and Hugh O'Neill on which jobs artificial intelligence will really replace. They built a desktop simulation to help keep the debate honest.
Is artificial intelligence failing to deliver automation, or starting to make workers obsolete? Anthony Townsend and Hugh O'Neill built a simulation to test the debate.

pieces.title: AI to Listen Better
pieces.author: John Della Volpe
pieces.dek: What hundreds of hours of conversations with New Yorkers reveal about everyday life — and how cities can earn trust.

posts.text: John Della Volpe says daily AI-led phone interviews with New Yorkers caught shifts that official data misses. Mentions of ICE tripled from spring to October. Mentions of the rent freeze spiked after the vote, then faded.
Read pollster John Della Volpe on building an AI interviewer in his own voice, and what 3,282 conversations with New Yorkers taught him about listening.
"I never had a person that actually cared enough to understand my circumstances." A New Yorker on being interviewed by AI, from John Della Volpe's account of what hundreds of hours of listening show.

pieces.title: AI to Amplify Civic Participation
pieces.author: Audrey Tang
pieces.dek: Connect residents with the city workers who can solve their problems. Don't replace those workers.

posts.text: Audrey Tang argues New York City should use AI to route residents to the city worker who owns their problem, and keep the thread open for follow-up. Her case: it puts people in front of workers, not in their place.
Read Audrey Tang on how New York City could use AI to close the gap 311 leaves open. She drew on Taiwan's Polis, Engaged California and Germany's SPRIND, and on her own call about an IDNYC.
"The answer to my question existed all along; there was simply no way for me to reach the person who had it." Audrey Tang on calling 311 about her IDNYC, and what AI could change.

pieces.title: Generate Economic Gains for Every New Yorker
pieces.author: Jared Giles
pieces.dek: Lessons from Amazon HQ2 for New York's AI economy

posts.text: Jared Giles argues New York City should negotiate with AI companies the way Arlington did with Amazon: performance-based incentives, strict enforcement and an AI Fund that shares the gains with residents.
Read Jared Giles on what Amazon HQ2 teaches New York City about the AI economy. Giles says city government has focused on safety and has not yet negotiated for economic gains.

Could an AI Fund pay for CityFHEPS, bigger kindergarten savings accounts and support for workers displaced by automation? Jared Giles lays out how it could work, modeled on the JFK Airport community program.

pieces.title: AI to Connect Neighbors
pieces.author: Dominic Ramos-Ruiz
pieces.dek: Most civic technology focuses on making cities more efficient, overlooking the relationships that hold them together.

posts.text: Dominic Ramos-Ruiz argues that city engagement efforts hear residents one at a time and miss the neighbors beside them. AI, he says, could connect people whose concerns overlap, if both opt in.
Read Dominic Ramos-Ruiz on how AI could help New Yorkers meet the neighbors they share a building, a block or a grievance with, and what it takes for people to trust the tools.
"AI cannot manufacture human connection, but it can give us more reasons to recognize each other." From Dominic Ramos-Ruiz on technology and neighborhood life.

pieces.title: AI to Shred Government Paperwork
pieces.author: Rohit Aggarwala
pieces.dek: Employees need not get bogged down by red tape.

posts.text: Rohit Aggarwala argues the Mamdani administration should train AI on three years of approved and rejected city forms, then use it to check paperwork before it is submitted.
Read Rohit Aggarwala on using AI to catch mistakes in internal government forms, before a rejected hire memo or contract sends the work back to the start.
"The goal is not to replace human government with government by AI, but to use AI to check forms before they are submitted." Rohit Aggarwala on speeding up New York City government.

pieces.title: AI to Help Lift People Up
pieces.author: Sam Schaeffer
pieces.dek: How technology helps with reentry — and can assist with other complicated social services work

posts.text: Sam Schaeffer argues AI should supplement human job coaches, not replace them. His group built a voice coach people reach by phone because asking them to download an app cut engagement.

Read Sam Schaeffer, who leads the Center for Employment Opportunities, on how an AI phone coach helped a man prepare for his first job interview after prison, and what it couldn't do when he was laid off.
Could a tool built to help people prepare for parole hearings make parole boards more skeptical of them? Sam Schaeffer writes about why his organization is asking that before it launches one.

pieces.title: The Best Street Safety Fix New York Isn’t Using
pieces.author: Sara Lind
pieces.dek: London slashed casualties on residential streets without banning cars or removing parking.

posts.text: London cut casualties on residential streets without banning cars or removing parking, writes Sara Lind. She says New York City is not using the fix.
Read Sara Lind on drivers cutting through residential blocks in all five boroughs, and on the street safety fix from London that New York City has not tried.
"That chaos isn't just unpleasant; it costs lives." Sara Lind writes on the traffic moving onto New York City's local streets, and what London did about its own.

pieces.title: Tough Truths About Integration and Education
pieces.author: Daniel Weisberg
pieces.dek: Should equalizing New York City schools' ethnic and racial compositions really be a top priority?

posts.text: Daniel Weisberg argues that before New York City redraws school boundaries again, it should settle what outcomes integration is meant to achieve. Diversity, racial balance and school quality are different things.
Read Daniel Weisberg on integration and education, written in response to Nikole Hannah-Jones' essay on her daughter's Brooklyn schooling and her questions to Chancellor Kamar Samuels.
Should equalizing New York City schools' ethnic and racial compositions be a top priority? Daniel Weisberg takes up the question and asks what outcomes the City actually wants.

pieces.title: A New Rec Center Comes to Play
pieces.author: Alyssa Katz
pieces.dek: An ambitious new facility in Brooklyn pushes back on lightweight expectations about what's possible.

posts.text: Alyssa Katz describes a new public recreation center in Brooklyn that pushes back on lightweight expectations: a competition-size pool, a packed class schedule, and a $150 annual membership, free for anyone 24 or under.
Read Alyssa Katz on the Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center in Flatbush, from the keytag neighbors rave about to the swimsuit-drying machines that tell patrons they matter.
"Digital keypads secure the lockers, attendants spritz tile to a shine and swimsuit-drying machines say to patrons: you matter." Alyssa Katz on Brooklyn's new Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center.

pieces.title: How Strong Are the Winds at Mamdani’s Back?
pieces.author: Ross Barkan
pieces.dek: The mayor has been amazingly fortunate so far. The good luck may not last.

posts.text: Ross Barkan argues Zohran Mamdani has had far better tailwinds than Bill de Blasio did: a friendlier Albany, a weaker police union and no Eric Garner. The risks, he says, are a Wall Street downturn and ICE.
Read Ross Barkan on how Mamdani's first year compares with de Blasio's, and what could end the good run. Barkan discloses that Mamdani managed his 2018 campaign for office.
What happens if the local economy slows and Mamdani has to make cuts his base reviles? Ross Barkan on the luck that has carried the mayor so far, and where it could run out.

pieces.title: Let’s Be Demanding of Government, but Not Cheaply Cynical About It
pieces.author: Vishaan Chakrabarti
pieces.dek: Connecting the dots between the midterms and better scaffolding=

posts.text: Vishaan Chakrabarti argues that cynicism about government is a vicious circle: the more we pile on petty critiques of every shortfall, the slower and more imperfect public work becomes.
Read Vishaan Chakrabarti, an architect who works mostly for government, on the mock-up sidewalk sheds at Broadway and Chambers Street and the online snark that greeted them.
"People see the widespread failures brought on by our collective shortsightedness, and then become jaded when we try to fix any of it." Vishaan Chakrabarti on cynicism and the midterms.

pieces.title: Is Zohran Mamdani’s Coalition Reshaping American Politics?
pieces.author: Richard Florida
pieces.dek: The midterm election results may signal that a deeper shift is underway.

posts.text: Richard Florida argues that the coalition behind the Democratic midterm landslide resembles the one Zohran Mamdani built to win the mayoralty: creative and service workers united by the cost of a decent life.
Read @richard_florida on whether Zohran Mamdani's coalition of creative and service workers is already reshaping American politics, and what the midterm results suggest about it.
"The midterm results suggest that coalition has legs and is already reshaping American politics." Richard Florida on what Zohran Mamdani's win in New York City may have previewed.

pieces.title: The Midterms Taught New York a Lesson About Character
pieces.author: Nicole Gelinas
pieces.dek: Like or loathe their policies, Hochul and Mamdani tend to behave like decent human beings. Blakeman, not so much.

posts.text: Nicole Gelinas argues Bruce Blakeman lost in part on character: he twice tried to use 9/11 for political points, and voters who paid attention noticed. Policy ideas were only part of it.
Read @nicolegelinas on why New York Republicans cannot beat Zohran Mamdani by attacking him as a person, and what Kathy Hochul and Mamdani did at the 9/11 ceremonies that Bruce Blakeman did not.
"Politicians are not just collections of platform planks; they are people." Nicole Gelinas on what the midterms showed about Bruce Blakeman, Hochul and Mamdani.

pieces.title: The Fiscal Significance of Mamdani’s Union Contracts
pieces.author: Tal Roded
pieces.dek: The agreements City Hall inks with organized labor will largely determine the magnitude of future budget gaps.

posts.text: Tal Roded argues that Mayor Mamdani should tie any pay raises for municipal unions to work rule reforms, because 3% annual raises would add billions to budget gaps that already exist.
Read Tal Roded on the DC 37 contract and what it means for the city budget. Roded says it will set the pattern for every other union, and Mayor Mamdani has to bargain hard.
How much does a 3% raise cost New York City? Tal Roded puts it at roughly $4 billion a year by year four, above what the budget plans for, on top of a $7.3 billion gap in fiscal year 2028.

pieces.title: There’s No Tenable Way To Integrate New York’s Schools from the Top Down
pieces.author: Tim DeRoche
pieces.dek: A tough truth that Zohran Mamdani and Nikole Hannah-Jones must reckon with

posts.text: Tim DeRoche argues that every route to forced integration of New York City schools is illegal, unpopular or both. The one option he sees left is to end zoned student assignment, as New Orleans did.
Read Tim DeRoche on why Mayor Mamdani can't integrate the city's schools from the top down, and what DeRoche says he could do instead about the zone map dividing P.S. 307 from the Roebling School.

Why can't children zoned to P.S. 307 attend the Roebling School less than a mile away? Tim DeRoche says it's an attendance zone line drawn and enforced by the Department of Education, and school choice has little to do with it.

pieces.title: It Wasn’t the Dutch Who Shaped New Amsterdam
pieces.author: Alan Mikhail
pieces.dek: A close reading of the letter that recorded the purchase of Manhattan from Native peoples

posts.text: The Schagen Letter is famous for the 60 guilders. Alan Mikhail argues its most important detail is a passing line about women giving birth to "some children," a sign that the colony might last.
Read Alan Mikhail on who actually built New Amsterdam: Catalina Trico, Anthony the Turk, Mayken van Angola and others who stayed for decades, long after the fur traders left.

Who were the real founders of the colony that became New York? Alan Mikhail says the people who stayed longest: "the enslaved, the rejected, the religiously othered, the hustlers, the rabble-rousers."

pieces.title: What Does Zohran Mamdani’s Office of Mass Engagement Really Do?
pieces.author: Sage Lattman
pieces.dek: A view from the pavement

posts.text: Sage Lattman went canvassing with Mayor Mamdani's Office of Mass Engagement and finds the events stay within the law. Whether they actually protect tenants, Lattman says, is unclear. The volunteers, though, are inspired.

Read @sagelattman on what Organize New York City does on the ground. Lattman attended two Talk to Tenants canvasses and a tenant organizing session, and asked a Columbia law professor whether any of it crosses a line.

"Government doesn't have to always be impartial if they think there's one side that needs help," says Columbia law professor Richard Briffault, on the Mamdani administration's tenant organizing, in Sage Lattman's reporting.

pieces.title: Did Federal Local Fiscal Recovery Funding Drive America’s Postpandemic Homicide Decline?
pieces.author: Ethan Doshi
pieces.dek: A close look at the evidence says it doesn't look likely.

posts.text: Cities that got more federal recovery money than similar cities in their state saw no bigger drop in homicide, finds Ethan Doshi. The biggest surges, he writes, produced the biggest declines.
Read Ethan Doshi on whether American Rescue Plan money drove the postpandemic homicide decline. He tested the theory across hundreds of cities and says the signal isn't there.
Why did homicide fall fastest in the cities that got the most federal money? Ethan Doshi says the formula sent money to the hardest-hit places, and those places were already due to fall back.

pieces.title: Taking Gun Violence Seriously
pieces.author: Philip J. Cook
pieces.dek: On Malcolm Gladwell's latest book, "The American Way of Killing"

posts.text: Philip J. Cook says Malcolm Gladwell is right that American police forces are too small, but wrong that trauma care explains the homicide numbers. Chicago shooting data shows why.
Read Philip J. Cook, who has researched American gun violence for 50 years, on Malcolm Gladwell's "The American Way of Killing": what the book gets right, and where he says it misses.
Did better trauma care keep the homicide rate from tripling? Philip J. Cook checked Gladwell's claim against Chicago shooting data and the National Crime Victimization Survey.

pieces.title: How Unchecked Immigration Enforcement Risks Making U.S. Cities Less Safe
pieces.author: Nayna Gupta
pieces.dek: ICE actions are harming trust between locals and police.

posts.text: Nayna Gupta argues that no amount of effective local policing can make up for what aggressive federal immigration enforcement does to public trust in police, and so to public safety.
Read Nayna Gupta on what happens when local police become a force multiplier for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and what New York City and other cities can do about it.

Does involving local police in immigration enforcement make cities safer? Nayna Gupta points to a new American Economic Review study: Hispanic victims reported fewer crimes and were more likely to become victims.

pieces.title: When ICE Comes to Town: The Role of Law, Local Police and Neighbors
pieces.author: Vital City
pieces.dek: Former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson, immigration researcher Austin Kocher and Documented reporter Eileen Grench on what police should do when an immigration operation comes to a city.

posts.text: Former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson says local police should keep a role when federal agents work their neighborhoods. Refusing to cooperate with ICE, he argues, is counterproductive for public safety.

Read researcher Austin Kocher on who ICE is arresting. He says all the growth in arrests since last summer came from people with no criminal charges or convictions, a gap he says the data shows against the rhetoric.

"When you're out on the streets, use your common sense." Jeh Johnson says he told ICE that as Homeland Security Secretary. Hear him, Austin Kocher and Eileen Grench on what police should do when ICE comes to a city.
